I-roles.prompt: Assign each duty (or claimed duty) to the role it actually belongs to. Some belong to no one at all.

d1-case-charter.brief: Ferncastle Labs is a twelve-person startup whose AI models forecast prescription demand for independent pharmacies. Its only governance so far is an informal understanding among the three co-founders. A national pharmaceutical wholesaler wants to build Ferncastle's forecasts into its ordering platform, but its procurement team will not sign until it sees a documented AI governance program. You are hired to create one — and, later on, to adapt it after Ferncastle licenses its models to pharmacy chains in the EU, Canada and Japan.
d1-case-charter.steps[0].why: An inventory establishes what actually exists, and every later decision — who owns governance, what people need to learn, what the policy must say — depends on that picture. Appointing an executive or running awareness sessions first sets people to work without a defined scope, and a policy written before the inventory is shaped by assumptions rather than by the models Ferncastle really runs.
d1-case-charter.steps[1].why: Governance should be proportionate to the organisation. A brief principles charter captures values the founders already hold, makes them reviewable, and adds a single gate for new work without slowing the team down. A dedicated governance executive is an expense Ferncastle can't yet justify, handing the whole function to outsiders leaves the company without in-house ownership, and a framework designed for a large enterprise would overwhelm a team of twelve.
d1-case-charter.steps[2].why: A federated structure resolves the pull between consistency and local fit: principles are set once at the centre, while regional groups tailor how they are applied to each jurisdiction's law and expectations. A single uniform policy can't bend to different legal regimes, fully independent country programs lose central oversight and coherence, and spreading ownership across teams and product leads leaves it unclear who is accountable when a regulator asks who signed off.
d1-case-charter.steps[3].why: Most technical staff work alongside AI systems without ever needing to build them, so converting every engineer into a model developer is neither role-based nor achievable. The other three belong in a sound program: training matched to each role and the governance structure, an ethics track that builds culture, and education for the end users who rely on the model's outputs.

d1-case-policies.brief: Verdant Health Analytics has run a mature privacy compliance program for years — breach protocols, a standing PIA process, vendor contracts — all built around its original SaaS product, which only ever stored and processed the health records customers gave it directly. Verdant is now embedding a generative-AI clinical-documentation assistant into that same product, and the compliance team wants to reuse as much of the existing stack as it can rather than build a parallel one from scratch. Engineering, meanwhile, is already fielding requests from clinicians who want to paste patient notes into public chatbots to save time.
d1-case-policies.steps[0].why: A PIA is already built to ask exactly the questions an AI system raises — what data goes in, what happens to individuals as a result — so extending it to cover training, fairness and explainability is a natural fit, not a rebuild. Penetration testing checks technical intrusion resistance, not algorithmic bias or legality; transfer assessments answer a narrower cross-border question; and staff training builds awareness but surfaces no system-specific risk at all.
d1-case-policies.steps[1].why: A legacy policy is written for static, direct data flows — what's collected, where it's stored — and never anticipated that a model's own outputs and inferences are a second, derived dataset that can be cross-referenced back to re-identify someone whose raw record was properly anonymized. A DPA, a named DPO and a breach-notification clock are all generic privacy-program hygiene any IT system needs; none of them is the AI-specific hole this scenario is pointing at.
d1-case-policies.steps[2].why: Every minute clinicians paste patient notes into a public tool, that text can leave Verdant's control entirely — used for the vendor's own training, logged, or exposed — which is the concrete harm a prohibition is actually preventing. Monetization strategy and hiring costs aren't privacy risks at all, and 'no time to train yet' describes a temporary resourcing gap, not a reason a leak of PHI is dangerous enough to justify blocking the tool outright.
d1-case-policies.steps[3].why: Folding AI rules into the existing privacy, security and ethics policies keeps governance unified and prevents the organization from running two sets of standards that can quietly drift apart — regulators and auditors expect AI to sit under the same accountability structure as everything else. The regulator-signaling argument is true but too narrow to carry the case on its own, and both the detail and speed arguments for a standalone document trade long-term cohesion for short-term convenience, which is exactly what creates the silos integration is meant to avoid.

d1-case-vendor-file.brief: Bramwell Mutual's claims division is evaluating third-party AI vendors to triage incoming insurance claims. Two finalists have made it to contract review, and a third vendor's model is already being eyed for the HR team's resume-screening pilot next quarter. Governance is asked to run the file: how much scrutiny each vendor actually needs, what to do when one won't show its work, what to do when the best model doesn't meet Bramwell's own security bar, and what belongs in the paperwork before any of them go live.
d1-case-vendor-file.steps[0].why: Third-party AI risk management works the same way internal risk management does: effort proportional to risk, checked on an ongoing basis rather than once at signing. A blanket biannual audit for every vendor is excessive and not scalable, financial stability alone ignores the actual harm an AI system can cause, and splitting technical risk from ethical risk (leaving the latter to contract text) treats two halves of the same evaluation as if they were unrelated.
d1-case-vendor-file.steps[1].why: If the policy says a risk assessment must happen before procurement and the vendor's refusal makes that assessment impossible, proceeding anyway breaks the organization's own governance framework — the defensible move is to walk away. Internal monitoring is a weak substitute for the assessment that never happened, carving out a policy exception undermines the policy for every future vendor, and an indemnification clause can shift financial liability but does nothing to fill the operational and ethical blind spot Bramwell is left with.
d1-case-vendor-file.steps[2].why: A sandbox is the compensating control built for precisely this situation — it lets Bramwell capture the model's performance while containing the exposure created by a vendor that can't meet the security bar directly. Waiving the requirement or writing a standing exception for 'reputable' vendors both erode the security standard for everyone else, while an outright block treats a workable containment problem as an unworkable one and may cost Bramwell a genuinely superior model for no defensible reason.
d1-case-vendor-file.steps[3].why: Risk in an AI system accumulates over its operating life: a screening model can start disadvantaging certain applicants well after the contract is signed, so the agreement needs a continuing reporting obligation and an agreed way to retire the system when it stops being fit for purpose. A component schedule is a one-off licensing check, full access to code and training data is something vendors rarely grant and adds little when monitoring is robust, and fixed service thresholds measure a point in time rather than the drift and fairness problems that develop later.

i-rl-01.text: Selects the training data and runs pre-release bias tests, then documents how the system functions for the people who will operate it
i-rl-01.why: Build-stage duties — curating data, fairness testing before release, and documentation for operators — sit with whoever builds the system. This is distinct from the ongoing, in-context monitoring the operating organization runs once the system is live.

i-rl-02.text: Embeds bias-testing tools and explainability features directly into the model while it is being trained, then chooses how to trade off accuracy against fairness
i-rl-02.why: Technical safeguards built into the model itself — 'governance by design' — are a build-time choice about architecture and training, made before the system ever reaches a live environment.

i-rl-03.text: Records where the training data came from and explains why a particular model architecture was chosen over the alternatives
i-rl-03.why: Data lineage and design-rationale records are artifacts of the build process itself — they explain choices made before the system exists, not how it performs once running.

i-rl-04.text: Monitors live performance and drift in its own operating context and audits accuracy on an ongoing basis
i-rl-04.why: Operational integrity in a specific context is the distinguishing duty here — not the design choices behind the model, which belong to whoever built it before it ever reached this context.

i-rl-05.text: Integrates the model into a production environment and sets up the monitoring that will watch it once it is running there
i-rl-05.why: Standing the system up in production and instrumenting it is an operational act, separate from the training and testing that produced the model in the first place.

i-rl-06.text: Carries the primary liability when an unvalidated third-party system is put into a hospital's care pathway without independent validation first
i-rl-06.why: Liability follows the decision to put an unvalidated system into a live setting, which is the operating organization's call — the original builder is not the one who chose to skip validation before use.

i-rl-07.text: Interacts with the AI system in real-world situations and is often the first to notice something has gone wrong
i-rl-07.why: Proximity to the live outcome — noticing bias, errors, or drift as it actually happens — is the front-line role, distinct from the organization that operates and monitors the system as a whole.

i-rl-08.text: Interprets the system's recommendation and makes the final, informed decision based on it
i-rl-08.why: Applying judgment to a specific output and deciding what to do with it is a point-of-use act, not the operational monitoring or design work that happens elsewhere in the lifecycle.

i-rl-09.text: Serves as the escalation point when one team wants to ship an AI feature quickly but another team raises regulatory concerns about it
i-rl-09.why: Reconciling competing functional interests day to day is an operational, cross-functional job — narrower in scope than the specialized moral-and-societal review of high-impact use cases, and it doesn't set enterprise risk appetite the way the top of the organization does.

i-rl-10.text: Decides which of several competing AI proposals gets resourced first, weighing risk level against strategic priority and available resources
i-rl-10.why: Prioritizing use cases against risk and resources is a standing, cross-functional operating decision — distinct from the one-off moral review a specialized body gives a single high-impact case, and distinct from the top-level appetite-setting that funds the whole program.

i-rl-11.text: Asks 'should we build this system at all?' rather than only 'can we build it?' for a proposed use case
i-rl-11.why: Weighing whether a use case is right, not just permissible, is the specialized moral-and-societal review — narrower and deeper than the operational prioritization a cross-functional body runs across all proposals.

i-rl-12.text: Requires bias audits and corrective measures for a hiring tool before it is approved, weighing fairness against harm to particular groups
i-rl-12.why: Independent review of disproportionate harm to a protected population is the specialized ethical-review function — distinct from the cross-functional committee's broader operational sign-off.

i-rl-13.text: Provides independent advice on whether a proposal fits the organization's stated values, even in cases where it is already technically legal
i-rl-13.why: Judging a gray area that clears the legal bar but still raises questions of public trust is exactly the reflective function a specialized moral body exists for, separate from legal or operational sign-off.

i-rl-14.text: Sets the organization's AI risk appetite and decides whether the overall strategy favors innovation speed or strict compliance
i-rl-14.why: Setting the tone and tolerance for risk across the whole organization sits above any single review body — committees and boards operate within the appetite that gets set here, not the other way around.

i-rl-15.text: Approves the overall governance framework and allocates the budget that funds it
i-rl-15.why: Approving and funding the framework itself is a top-of-organization act of legitimacy and resourcing, distinct from the day-to-day operation of that framework by the bodies it funds.

i-rl-16.text: Confirms the AI strategy aligns with external expectations such as industry standards and regulatory requirements, not only with internal business goals
i-rl-16.why: Aligning the organization's overall direction with the outside world is a strategic act at the top, distinct from the operational compliance-checking that legal and risk teams carry out underneath that direction.

i-rl-17.text: Remains fully liable for a system's compliance with regulations even after it has been handed over to whoever runs it now
i-rl-17.why: Documented false: the original builder does not remain fully liable once operation passes to another role. Liability is shared and tracks each role's actual responsibilities — the operating organization takes on the liability that comes with operating the system.

i-rl-18.text: Sits inside the AI development lifecycle as a standing participant, approving each phase before the next one can proceed
i-rl-18.why: Documented false: this describes external oversight bodies, and oversight/enforcement from outside is not the same as being an engaged participant inside the lifecycle stages themselves, alongside data architects, socio-cultural and technical experts, and legal/privacy specialists.
